1. How to use this guide and what the manual covers

The manual is mostly labeled images. This guide keeps every manual finding, then adds the bedside context you need on rotations. beyond source marks what was added.

Manual goals: correct pre-settings, correct anatomy, recognize pathology, measure IMT and LVEF, understand emergency uses (eFAST, venous, lung).

2. Physics and knobology

beyond source The manual lists physics as an objective but gives no detail. These are the points that change what you see on the screen.

ConceptRulePractical effect
Speed of sound in soft tissueAbout 1540 m/s assumed by the machineDepth is calculated from echo return time
Frequency vs depthHigher frequency = better resolution, more attenuation, less depthSuperficial structures: high frequency. Deep: low frequency
EchogenicityBright (hyperechoic) = strong reflectors (bone, calcium, fat, air interfaces). Dark (hypoechoic) = weak. Black (anechoic) = fluidFluid is black; cysts, bladder, vessels, effusions
GainOverall brightness of the returning signalToo high = washed out. Too low = lose pathology
DepthHow far the display reachesSet so the target sits in the middle of the screen
FocusNarrows beam at chosen levelPlace at or just below the target
Time gain compensation (TGC)Gain at selected depthsFixes dark far field from attenuation
PresetMachine settings for exam typeChoose the right preset first (manual: correct pre-settings)
ModeWhat it showsUse
B-mode (2D)Grayscale anatomyAlmost everything
M-modeOne line through timeLVEF D and S diameters, lung sliding (seashore vs barcode), IVC
Color DopplerFlow toward (red) or away (blue) from probe, BARTRegurgitation, calculus twinkling, vessel patency
Spectral Doppler (PW / CW)Velocity over timeValve gradients, aortic insufficiency
Power DopplerFlow presence, no directionSlow flow, inflammation, testes

Probe marker convention: marker to the patient right or cephalad (toward head); the screen marker is at the upper left of the image (except cardiac in some settings, so verify on your machine).

3. Probes, planes and artifacts

Probe choice beyond source

ProbeFrequencyFootprintUse
LinearAbout 5-15 MHzFlat, wideVascular (carotid, DVT, veins), MSK (shoulder, knee, tendons), lung pleural line, procedures
CurvilinearAbout 2-5 MHzCurved, wideAbdomen: gallbladder, liver, kidneys, bladder, aorta, FAST, thoracentesis/paracentesis
Phased arrayAbout 1-5 MHzSmallCardiac (between ribs), also FAST and lung
EndocavitaryAbout 5-9 MHzSmall, curvedTransvaginal and transrectal

Planes

  • Longitudinal (long axis): along the structure; marker toward head for most views.
  • Transverse (short axis): across the structure; marker to the patient right.
  • In-plane needle: whole needle shaft seen (long axis). Out-of-plane: only a dot (short axis).

Artifacts beyond source

ArtifactLooks likeSeen withClinical meaning
Posterior acoustic shadowingDark band behind a strong reflectorGallstones, renal stones, boneManual: calculi = hyperechoic focus with shadowing
Posterior acoustic enhancementBright band behind fluidCysts, bladder, gallbladderConfirms fluid-filled
AnisotropyTendon looks falsely dark when beam is not perpendicularTendons (biceps, supraspinatus, patellar)Manual: keep beam perpendicular to avoid mistaking it for tendinopathy
ReverberationEvenly spaced repeating linesPleura, bladder wallA-lines on lung
Comet tail / ring-downNarrow bright streakPleura, metal, gasB-lines on lung; twinkling behind stones on color Doppler
Mirror imageDuplicate below a strong reflectorDiaphragm / liverDo not mistake for a mass
Edge shadowingDark streaks from curved edgesGallbladder, cystsNormal

4. Musculoskeletal

Manual chapter 1. Competency: knee (lateral transverse) and shoulder (posterior transverse).

Cellulitis: hypoechoic or anechoic edematous subcutaneous areas (arrows). Manual figure.
Intramuscular hematoma: hypoechoic or anechoic fluid area. Looks like abscess, so trauma history is needed to tell them apart. Manual figure.
FindingUltrasound appearanceKey point
CellulitisHypoechoic or anechoic edematous subcutaneous areas'Cobblestone' pattern is a classic extension beyond source; look for a drainable pocket
Intramuscular hematomaHypo- or anechoic fluid area within muscleHistory of trauma separates it from abscess (similar appearance)
TendinopathyAcute: thickened tendon, hypoechoic from inflammation and edemaKeep the beam perpendicular, or anisotropy mimics it
FractureCortical break or step-off, hematomaListed by the manual; often found by focal pain on probe beyond source
Joint effusionAnechoic fluid in the recessKnee suprapatellar and shoulder posterior recess
Tendon, asymptomatic vs symptomatic side (thicker, darker tendon on the symptomatic side). Manual figure.
Posterior shoulder: infraspinatus muscle and tendon, humeral head, posterior joint recess. Manual figure.

Shoulder, posterior transverse (competency)

  • Probe over the posterior shoulder below the scapular spine.
  • Identify: deltoid and infraspinatus (muscle/tendon), humeral head (bright curved cortex), articular cartilage (thin dark rim), posterior joint recess.
  • Effusion = anechoic fluid in the posterior recess beyond source.

Knee, lateral transverse (competency)

  • Linear probe, knee slightly flexed.
  • Look at the suprapatellar recess for anechoic fluid; compare with the other side beyond source.
  • Manual: ultrasound can show the effusion that MRI also shows (see section 12).

Rotation pearls beyond source

  • Hot swollen joint: ultrasound confirms effusion and marks the safest needle path for aspiration.
  • Soft tissue lump: fluid pocket on ultrasound before incision and drainage.
  • Always compare with the opposite side and check for anisotropy by tilting the probe.

5. Cardiac

Manual chapter 2. Competency: parasternal long axis (PLAX) LVEF.

PLAX B-mode view. Manual figure.
PLAX M-mode at the mitral valve level: E-point, A-point, anterior and posterior mitral leaflets, interventricular septum, RV and LV. Manual figure.

The four standard cardiac views (Butterfly cardiac protocol)

Butterfly cardiac protocol card: PLAX, PSAX, A4C and subcostal views with probe positions. 1 LV, 2 RV, 3 LA, 4 RA, 5 aortic valve at the aortic root, 6 mitral valve, 7 descending thoracic aorta, 8 liver, 9 papillary muscles.
ViewPatient positionProbe placement and marker
PLAX (parasternal long axis)Slight left lateral decubitus (LLD)Just left of the sternum, third or fourth intercostal space; marker toward the patient's right shoulder
PSAX (parasternal short axis)Slight LLDFrom PLAX rotate the probe 90° clockwise (marker toward the left shoulder); fan from apex to base
A4C (apical 4-chamber)Slight LLDFrom PSAX slide lateral to the left side; rotate clockwise with the marker at 3 o'clock; aim toward the right shoulder
SubcostalSupineInferior and deep to the xiphoid, marker to the patient's left; steep angle aiming up toward the heart

beyond source Protocol card from a handheld-device manufacturer; the competency uses PLAX for LVEF, but the other three views are the standard POCUS cardiac set. Marker orientation can differ by machine and preset, so confirm on the screen.

LVEF from M-mode or B-mode

LVEF = [LV diameter (diastole) − LV diameter (systole)] / LV diameter (diastole) measured in PLAX at the mitral valve level.

  • Diastolic diameter (D) is the widest, systolic (S) the narrowest, at the tips of the mitral leaflets.
  • Normal LVEF about 52-72% (men) and 54-74% (women) beyond source.
  • Quick bedside estimate: E-point septal separation (EPSS) above about 7 mm suggests reduced EF beyond source.

LV hypertrophy (LVH)

  • Manual case: 20 years of hypertension and shortness of breath; LV wall 14 mm, interventricular septum (IVS) 13 mm, small pericardial effusion.
  • Normal wall thickness: below 12 mm (manual).

Aortic insufficiency

Color Doppler, aortic insufficiency: diastolic regurgitant jet. Manual figure.
Continuous-wave Doppler, aortic regurgitation. Manual figure.
  • Clinical: diastolic murmur.
  • Color Doppler shows a diastolic regurgitant jet; spectral Doppler shows flow above the baseline in diastole.
  • Severity (jet width, pressure half-time) is a formal echo question beyond source.

Quick cardiac checks on rotations beyond source

QuestionViewFinding
Pericardial effusionPLAX, subxiphoid, apicalAnechoic rim around the heart; tamponade = RA/RV diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC
Gross LV functionPLAX, apical 4-chamberNormal squeeze, wall thickening, septal motion
RV strainApical 4-chamberRV larger than LV, septal flattening (PE suspicion)
Cardiac standstillSubxiphoid or parasternalNo organized wall motion during arrest (does not alone justify stopping)

6. Lung and pleura

Competency: normal lung A-lines and B-lines. Pneumothorax signs are the key eFAST thoracic findings.

A-lines: horizontal repeating lines below the pleura (reverberation). Manual figure.
B-lines: vertical streaks from the pleura to the bottom of the screen. Manual figure.
M-mode, normal lung: seashore sign (waves above, sand below). Manual figure.
M-mode, no lung sliding: barcode sign. Manual figure.
Annotated normal lung (Butterfly): red = rib shadows, blue = pleural line between the ribs, yellow-green = A-lines repeating at equal depth below the pleural line.
Annotated B-line (Butterfly): red = rib shadow, blue = pleural line, yellow = B-line running from the pleural line to the bottom of the screen.
  • Ribs appear as curved bright lines with dark shadows behind them; the pleural line sits just deeper, between the rib shadows ('bat sign') beyond source.
  • A-lines are horizontal, evenly spaced copies of the pleural line.
  • A B-line starts at the pleural line, is vertical and laser-like, erases the A-lines and moves with lung sliding beyond source.
SignMeaning
A-lines (horizontal)Air-filled lung is normal; also in pneumothorax if no sliding
B-lines (vertical)Fluid or thickened septa in the lung; beyond source: three or more per view is abnormal; one or two can be normal
Seashore sign (M-mode)Normal lung sliding
Barcode sign (M-mode)Absent lung sliding: pneumothorax, but also not specific
Lung point beyond sourceEdge of the pneumothorax where sliding appears and disappears; about 100% specific

Interpretation by pattern beyond source

PatternLikely
A-lines + lung slidingNormal, or asthma/COPD
Diffuse bilateral B-lines + slidingPulmonary edema (cardiogenic)
Focal B-lines or consolidationPneumonia, contusion
A-lines, absent sliding, no B-lines, lung pointPneumothorax
A-lines + normal lung + DVTPulmonary embolism
Anechoic fluid above diaphragmPleural effusion

Causes of absent sliding without pneumothorax beyond source: right mainstem intubation, apnea, pleural adhesions, large bullae. Always scan several spaces.

7. Hepatobiliary

Manual chapter 3. Competency: gallstones.

Gallbladder with thickened wall and sludge. Manual figure.
Sonographic Murphy sign: tenderness under the probe over the gallbladder. Manual figure.
Acute cholecystitis findingDetail
Wall thickeningMore than 3 mm
Pericholecystic fluidFluid rim around the gallbladder
Stones and sludgeStones echogenic with posterior shadowing
Sonographic Murphy signMaximal tenderness under the probe on the gallbladder

MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease)

Healthy liver, simple fat, steatohepatitis, cirrhosis. Fat stages are reversible, cirrhosis is irreversible. Manual figure.
B-mode steatosis grades: none, mild, moderate, severe. Manual figure.
  • Grade by liver echogenicity compared with the renal cortex.
  • Healthy liver is similar to or slightly brighter than the cortex; steatosis makes it brighter and deeper structures harder to see beyond source.

Also listed by the manual: biliary obstruction, benign hepatic lesions

  • Biliary obstruction beyond source: dilated common bile duct (above about 6 mm in an adult, interpret with age), dilated intrahepatic ducts, look for stone or mass.
  • Benign hepatic lesions beyond source: simple cyst (anechoic with enhancement), hemangioma (small, bright, well defined).
  • Sonography cannot exclude cholangitis or all stones; correlate with labs and further imaging.

8. Kidney and bladder

Manual chapter 4. Competency: kidney calculi.

Right kidney, sagittal. Manual figure.
Kidney sizes and views in CKD and normal comparison. Manual figure.
FindingAppearance
Normal kidney beyond sourceLength about 9-12 cm; cortex darker than liver/spleen; central sinus bright
CKDCortex echogenicity increases; cortex thickness and kidney size decrease as disease advances
HydronephrosisDilated collecting system, graded mild, moderate, severe (anechoic branching fluid, then rounded calyces, then thin parenchyma)
CalculiHyperechoic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing; color Doppler 'twinkling' comet-tail artifact
Normal, mild, moderate, severe hydronephrosis. Manual figure (Sheehan & Kelly 2022).

Bladder

Bladder, supine (arrow). Manual figure.
Bladder, transverse, pre-void, with color Doppler (arrow). Manual figure.
  • Views: right kidney sagittal, bladder supine, bladder transverse, pre-void bladder.
  • Bladder is anechoic with posterior enhancement; measure in two planes for volume beyond source.
  • Hydronephrosis plus flank pain or AKI: look for a stone, obstruction, or a full bladder (retention) beyond source.

9. Carotid, aorta, veins

Carotid IMT and plaque

Longitudinal and transverse CCA: IMT, IJV. Manual figure.
IMT measured at the posterior wall of the distal common carotid on gray scale; software estimates mean IMT over 10 mm (example 0.8 mm). Manual figure.
  • Measure the posterior wall of the distal common carotid artery (CCA); mean IMT is averaged over 10 mm.
  • IMT thickening progresses to plaque (manual).
  • Plaque beyond source (Mannheim consensus): focal structure encroaching at least 0.5 mm or 50% of surrounding IMT, or thickness above 1.5 mm.
Carotid arteriosclerosis: plaque in the carotid bulb, with ICA, ECA and IJV. Manual figure.

Abdominal aorta

Aorta measured proximal, mid, distal. Manual figure.
Infrarenal aorta 4.46 cm just above the bifurcation = AAA. Manual figure.
  • Normal: below 3 cm; measure proximal, mid and distal (outer wall to outer wall) beyond source.
  • AAA (abdominal aortic aneurysm): 3 cm or more. Manual example 4.46 cm.
  • Unstable patient with pain/hypotension and AAA = surgical emergency beyond source.

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

DVT is the main source of pulmonary embolism. Manual figure.
Femoral vein: normal (compressible) vs common femoral with thrombus (incompressible). Manual figure.
Popliteal vein compression, uncompressed and compressed. Manual figure.
CriterionFinding
Compression (first line)Completely incompressible vein on transverse view = obstructive DVT
Partial compressionNon-obstructive DVT
LumenHypoechoic focus in the lumen
Color DopplerColor filling defect in the lumen
  • Manual competency: popliteal vein compression.
  • Bedside 2-point or 3-point exam: common femoral, superficial femoral/deep femoral junction, popliteal beyond source.
  • Compress with enough pressure to flatten the artery slightly; vein collapse = normal.

10. eFAST

FAST = focused assessment with sonography for trauma. eFAST adds thoracic ultrasound.

eFAST probe positions (Knoop et al., Atlas of Emergency Medicine, 4th ed.). Manual figure.
StepViewLook for
1Right upper quadrant (RUQ)Free fluid between liver and kidney (Morison pouch) and above the diaphragm
2Left upper quadrant (LUQ)Fluid between spleen and kidney, around spleen, above the diaphragm
3PelvicFluid behind or around the bladder
4Cardiac (subxiphoid)Pericardial effusion
5Lung (anterior chest)Sliding (pneumothorax), pleural fluid
Bleeding, liver/spleen laceration, bowel perforation, kidney injury. Manual figure.
FindingMeaning
HemoperitoneumFree fluid (blood)
PneumoperitoneumFree air (perforation)
Pericardial effusion / tamponadeBlood in pericardium
Hemothorax / pneumothoraxFluid or air in the chest
Organ lacerationLiver, spleen, kidney
Bowel perforationFree fluid or air

Pitfalls beyond source

  • A negative FAST does not rule out injury (retroperitoneal and hollow organ injuries are missed); repeat it if the patient is unstable.
  • Free fluid in the pelvis: bladder should be full for best visualization.
  • Positive FAST in an unstable patient usually means the operating room, not CT.

11. IVC and volume status

IVC subcostal views and the IVC collapsibility index. Manual figure.

IVCCI (%) = (max IVC diameter in expiration − min IVC diameter in inspiration) / max IVC diameter in expiration × 100 (manual).

  • Used to evaluate blood volume.
  • Measure in long axis about 1-2 cm from the right atrium junction, perpendicular to the vessel beyond source.
IVC beyond sourceCollapse with sniffEstimated right atrial pressure
2.1 cm or lessMore than 50%3 mmHg (0-5) normal
2.1 cm or lessLess than 50%8 mmHg (5-10)
More than 2.1 cmMore than 50%8 mmHg (5-10)
More than 2.1 cmLess than 50%15 mmHg (10-20) high

Limits beyond source: ventilated patients, athletes, increased abdominal pressure and heart failure with preserved EF make it unreliable; use it with the clinical picture and lung B-lines, not alone.

12. Ultrasound-guided procedures

Manual chapter 6.

Ascites with bowel loops. Manual figure.
Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis: pleural fluid, diaphragm, needle. Manual figure.
ProcedureManual guidance
ParacentesisFind the largest fluid pocket, track the needle tip, watch the fluid change
ThoracentesisLocate pleural fluid above the diaphragm, track the needle, watch the fluid change
Shoulder / knee aspirationNeedle seen on longitudinal and transverse views of the joint
Vascular accessOut-of-plane (transverse, needle seen as a dot) vs in-plane (longitudinal, whole needle seen)
Needle in joint, longitudinal and transverse. Manual figure.
Knee effusion on B-mode vs MRI. Manual figure.
Depth rule: a needle entering at an angle travels farther than the vertical depth d (about 1.4 x d at 45 degrees). Manual figure.
Needle out-of-plane (short axis, dot) and in-plane (long axis). Manual figure.

Procedure checklist beyond source

  • Scan first and mark the site, or perform dynamic (real-time) guidance.
  • Use a sterile probe cover and gel; in-plane view for the whole needle.
  • Avoid vessels with color Doppler, especially the inferior epigastric artery (paracentesis) and the intercostal neurovascular bundle below each rib (thoracentesis).
  • Confirm the tip before injecting or aspirating; look for post-procedure pneumothorax after thoracentesis.
  • Standard consent, time-out and sterile technique still apply.
